blocks.content: You almost certainly typed a domain name to get here, not a raw number. But every single piece of actual routing you have learned about across the ipv4-vs-ipv6, cidr, subnetting, and routing-fundamentals topics in this module works entirely with IP addresses, never domain names at all. This closing topic of the module makes that relationship completely explicit.

This is deliberately a conceptual, closing topic, not the full mechanics. A dedicated DNS module immediately follows this one in the course, covering exactly how the translation itself actually happens, step by step. Here, the goal is simply making sure the relationship between the two is crystal clear before diving into those mechanics.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437574606-841925950.png
1. Two Completely Different Kinds of Identifiers
blocks.text: 1. Two Completely Different Kinds of Identifiers

blocks.content: A domain name, like google.com, and an IP address, like 142.250.183.14, are two genuinely different things serving two genuinely different purposes. A domain name exists purely for human convenience. An IP address is what the network itself actually uses to route data, exactly as covered throughout this whole module.
2. Why Domain Names Exist at All
blocks.text: 2. Why Domain Names Exist at All

blocks.content: Remembering, typing, and reliably sharing a string of numbers like 142.250.183.14 is genuinely hard for a human. Remembering google.com is effortless by comparison. Domain names exist purely to solve this human usability problem, they add zero actual routing capability of their own.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437574606-883773026.png
blocks.alt: Why Domain Names Exist at All

blocks.content: 3. DNS as a Phonebook

The Domain Name System, DNS, is exactly the lookup service that translates a human friendly domain name into the actual IP address a device needs to connect to. Think of it precisely like an old fashioned phonebook, translating a memorable person name into the actual phone number needed to reach them.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575112-235922222.png

{"headers":["Layer","What it is","Who or what uses it"],"rows":[["Domain name","A human friendly, memorable name","People, typed into a browser or shared casually"],["IP address","The actual network layer address","Routers, exclusively, for real forwarding decisions"]]}
4. Only IP Addresses Are Ever Actually Used for Routing
blocks.text: 4. Only IP Addresses Are Ever Actually Used for Routing

blocks.content: This is the single most important fact this topic exists to establish clearly. A router forwarding a packet, exactly as covered in the routing-fundamentals topic, only ever looks at IP addresses. It never sees, understands, or cares about domain names at all, those exist purely at a layer above actual routing, for human convenience only.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575113-770311607.png
blocks.alt: Only IP Addresses Are Ever Actually Used for Routing

blocks.title: A precise, important distinction
blocks.content: Domain names are a human interface layer, IP addresses are the actual network layer. DNS is specifically the bridge between these two, and once that translation happens, the domain name has done its job and disappears from the picture entirely.
5. The Order of Operations

When a browser wants to load a website, a DNS lookup genuinely has to happen FIRST, translating the typed domain name into an actual IP address, before any real connection can even begin. Only once that IP address is known does the actual connection, and everything covered in the Transport Layer and TCP Deep Dive modules, actually start.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575114-221245856.png
{"headers":["Step","What happens"],"rows":[["1: DNS lookup","Domain name translated into an actual IP address"],["2: Connection","The real connection uses only that IP address, never the name"]]}
6. A Genuine, Practical Benefit of This Separation
blocks.text: 6. A Genuine, Practical Benefit of This Separation

blocks.content: Because a domain name and an IP address are separate things linked only through a lookup, a domain name can stay exactly the same even while the actual server IP address behind it changes, a company migrating to new infrastructure, for instance. Users keep typing the exact same familiar name the whole time, completely unaware anything changed underneath.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575114-335809071.png
blocks.alt: A Genuine, Practical Benefit of This Separation

blocks.content: 7. One Address, Multiple Names

The relationship is not even strictly one to one. A single IP address can genuinely be reached through several different domain names at once, each one resolving to that exact same underlying address. This flexibility is a direct, natural consequence of domain names and IP addresses being two separate, independently managed systems linked only by DNS lookups.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575114-38660692.png

blocks.title: Closing out this module
blocks.content: Across this module, IPv4 and IPv6 covered the addresses themselves, public and private plus NAT covered how they get shared, CIDR and subnetting covered how ranges get described and divided, routing fundamentals covered how packets actually find their way, and this final topic ties it all back to the human friendly names people actually type.
8. What Comes Next

This topic deliberately stayed at the conceptual level, domain names and IP addresses are different things, DNS bridges them, and only IP addresses are ever actually used for routing. The dedicated DNS module immediately following this one goes deep into exactly how that lookup happens step by step, the full resolution process, the hierarchy of servers involved, and how caching keeps it fast.
